syllabus.clause: Z-order (Morton) and Hilbert curves linearising multi-dimensional keys; geohash, S2 cells and H3 hexagons; Z-order in Delta Lake ZORDER BY and Hilbert curves in Delta liquid clustering → Data Engineering §6.3.

at.step: Z-order interleaves each coordinate’s own bits, one bit from each axis in turn, into a single z-value. Connecting the z-values in order traces a recursively Z-shaped path, and the whole construction visits every one of the grid’s cells exactly once.

A Hilbert curve’s own recursive construction — each quadrant visited in an order and orientation chosen so the path never has to jump across a boundary it’s about to re-enter — keeps the identical boundary pair adjacent in its ordering, where Z-order’s jump was large.

Three production systems fix one specific curve and cell shape over this same idea: geohash interleaves latitude and longitude Z-order-style into a base-thirty-two string; S2 projects the sphere onto a cube and runs a Hilbert curve on each of its six faces; H3 tiles the sphere in hexagons instead of squares, because a hexagon’s neighbours are all the same distance from its centre, where a square’s corner neighbours sit farther away than its edge neighbours.

items.item: Z-order/Morton code maps multidimensional data to one dimension by bit-interleaving, preserving locality with high probability

items.item: Once sorted by interleaved bits, any one-dimensional structure can index the result directly

at.step: The obvious ordering is row-major: number the cells left to right, row by row. It works as an ordering — every cell gets a distinct number — but two cells that are neighbours on the grid can land arbitrarily far apart in it, the moment they sit in different rows.

items.item: Z-order preserves locality well, but not perfectly, at every boundary

at.step: Near the grid’s own origin corner, Z-order’s ordering is already about as tight as row-major’s. But a step across a boundary — crossing from one quadrant into the next — can jump the ordering by far more than a single step.

items.item: A Hilbert curve preserves locality fairly well, one-directionally

items.item: Hilbert order is proposed over Z-order for multidimensional databases specifically because of better locality-preserving behavior

at.step: A Hilbert curve is built recursively instead of by simple bit-interleaving. Can a curve built this way avoid Z-order’s own boundary jump?

items.item: Geohash is built directly on the Z-order curve, encoded in base-32 text

items.item: The Hilbert advantage is not claimed universally: examples.py measures three real pairs and reports the honest case (near the grid's own origin) where Z-order ties row-major and Hilbert is not the smallest of the three.

k-d trees, quadtrees/octrees and R-trees are named only as the skipped alternative family (building a new multi-dimensional tree shape) and are not built or benchmarked against Z-order/Hilbert in this topic, per the chapter plan's own skip list.

Geohash, S2, and H3 are each sourced from their own official documentation (or Wikipedia for geohash, which states the Z-order relationship directly), not from a secondary blog summary, for the one design choice this topic states about each.

items.item: Delta Lake's own ZORDER BY and liquid clustering are named only in passing, per the chapter plan's own cross-domain link to this course's Data Engineering track (§6.3), not rebuilt here.

The boundary-crossing pairs were chosen by inspecting each pair's own binary coordinates for a shared high-bit flip, not by searching after the fact for whichever pair produced the largest-looking gap.

items.item: The BIGMIN/LITMAX range-search machinery that makes Z-order efficient for range queries is named, from the source's own caveat about imperfect locality, but not built — this topic's scope is the ordering and its measured locality, not range-query machinery on top of it.

This topic declines to build k-d trees, quadtrees, R-trees, or either approximate-nearest-neighbour family, consistent with the chapter plan's own skip list for all of §9.1's remaining structures and all of §9.2.

The Hilbert xy2d construction used in examples.py is the standard recursive public-domain algorithm (quadrant chosen by the two high bits, remaining bits rotated/reflected, recurse one level down); it is verified structurally (a full bijection) rather than quoted as text, since no fetched source reproduced the algorithm's own code as extractable plain text.
